Bacteria. They are single-celled prokaryotic microorganisms lacking a nucleus, constituting the majority of Earth's biomass and driving essential biogeochemical cycles. First observed by van Leeuwenhoek in the seventeenth century but truly understood only after germ-theory and microscopy advanced in the nineteenth century, bacteria are omnipresent in soil, water, air, and living organisms—both as partners in photosynthesis and digestion and as agents of disease and decay.

Bacteria are prokaryotes. They have no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles, and DNA floats freely in the nucleoid region. Energy production occurs on the cell membrane. Reproduction is rapid and asexual through binary fission, enabling bacterial populations to double every twenty minutes under ideal conditions. This is why antibiotics must stop reproduction before it accelerates. Photosynthetic bacteria, particularly cyanobacteria, produce much of Earth's oxygen and drove the Great Oxidation Event. Non-photosynthetic bacteria are heterotrophs, consuming organic matter.

Bacteria possess a cell wall made of peptidoglycan in gram-positive species or lipopolysaccharide in gram-negative bacteria. This structure is the target of many antibiotics like penicillin. Horizontal gene transfer allows bacteria to acquire antibiotic resistance and other traits from neighboring cells, enabling rapid adaptation and representing a major public-health challenge. Bacteria vastly outnumber all other life by biomass. The human microbiome, found in the gut, skin, and respiratory tract, contains trillions of bacterial cells vital to digestion, immunity, and health.

Each bacterium is one cell. Binary fission produces two genetically identical daughters, enabling exponential population growth. Bacteria exhibit enormous metabolic diversity. Some are autotrophs making food via photosynthesis or chemosynthesis, while others are heterotrophs consuming organic matter. The human microbiome bacterial composition changes with diet, antibiotics, and health status. Dysbiosis, or an imbalanced microbiome, is linked to inflammatory diseases, obesity, and mental health disorders. Bacteria connect fundamentally to prokaryotes as the domain containing them, to cells as the simplest cellular life form, and to the concept of microorganisms themselves.
